evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied Midwestern teen discovers she’s a shape-shifting lab experiment and must outrun a biotech cover-up before the body she thinks is hers disappears for good.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and commercially legible: a teen identity thriller with body-swap stakes, a secret-corporate conspiracy, and a strong emotional spine. The audience is real and broad enough for streaming or genre theatrical, though the material is still more targeted than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands in the opening pages with the girl fleeing the woods, the shapeshift reveal, and the later twist that she may not be Ava at all. The script keeps the premise clean even as it escalates into memory theft, corporate cover-up, and identity collapse.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison is a strong lead because she’s vulnerable, funny, morally stubborn, and then forced into terrifying self-redefinition. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and David all have distinct energies that create playable relationships, especially once the script turns the mother-daughter bond into the emotional anchor.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar shapeshifter premise and makes the identity mechanics emotionally specific: touch-based copying, memory bleed, and the devastating reveal that the protagonist’s self-concept is built on stolen memory. The final act’s moral collision between survival and selfhood gives it real boldness.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The piece keeps escalating through clear set pieces: the roadside chase, the school confrontation, the mall identity scramble, the lab reveal, and the warehouse/lab climax. Once the rules are established, each sequence pushes the story into a new pressure point rather than repeating the same beat.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central twist — that the girl who thinks she is Ava is actually Madison, and that Ava exists separately — is both surprising and emotionally inevitable once the necklace, memory gaps, and body changes are in play. That combination of genre mechanics and identity grief is the script’s sharpest original move.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The small-town setting is specific and story-generating: burger joint, school, mall, townhouse development, forest edge, and secret lab all feel connected by a single corporate takeover. The world is strongest when it shows how a biotech operation can hide inside ordinary civic spaces and social media noise.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a recognizable tone: teen-movie banter colliding with body-horror panic and corporate paranoia. It’s not subtle, but it is distinct, especially in the way jokes about trucks and Vassar sit beside mutilation, memory theft, and a burning lab.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the thriller engine is a deeper story about class resentment, self-worth, maternal sacrifice, and who gets to own a body. The Ava/Madison reveal and the David relationship suggest more emotional material than the plot initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script gets a lot of mileage out of Ava/June, Ava/Shannon, Ava/Liam, Ava/Priscilla, and Ava/David, with each pairing generating a different kind of tension. Even secondary figures like Mills and Wilma have enough texture to keep the ensemble from feeling disposable.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, high-school age, working-class suburban Midwestern teen; later revealed to be Madison in Ava’s body/form.
lead_characters.hook: Ava reads like the smart, self-conscious girl who thinks she’s trapped in the wrong life: bright, funny, image-aware, and quietly furious that she doesn’t feel chosen by the world. As the story unfolds, that identity becomes unstable in the most literal way possible, and the role turns into a performance of panic, adaptation, and moral clarity under total psychic collapse. The reveal that she is actually Madison gives the character a devastating second life: she’s not just discovering powers, she’s discovering that her whole self has been assembled from memory, trauma, and longing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Florence Pugh in Midsommar — a young performer gets to play wit, humiliation, terror, and then a full identity rupture. It’s the kind of role that lets an actor move from teen lead to serious genre star in one swing.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, working-class mother, tattooed, blue-collar, emotionally hardened but deeply protective.
lead_characters.hook: June is the kind of mom role that feels lived-in immediately: funny, overextended, defensive, and capable of surprising physical and emotional force when her kid is threatened. She starts as a chaotic single-parent presence and becomes the story’s emotional ballast once she reveals she can shapeshift too and has been carrying the same nightmare in silence. The role has real contradiction — practical and reckless, cynical and loving, compromised and heroic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Jodie Foster in Panic Room — a mother who can pivot from comic exasperation to ferocious protection without losing credibility. It gives an actor a meaty emotional engine and a late-story action turn.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, Ava’s best friend, teen peer, socially grounded and emotionally direct.
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the best-friend role that keeps the movie human: she’s the one who can call out Ava’s nonsense, keep the banter alive, and still be the person Ava trusts when reality starts to break. She’s not just comic relief; she’s the audience’s social anchor inside a story that keeps destabilizing identity and memory. Her loyalty gives the script warmth and makes the town feel inhabited rather than schematic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Auliʻi Cravalho in The Little Mermaid or Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart — a sharp, funny best friend who gets to be the emotional truth-teller. It’s a role that can break out on chemistry and timing.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 40s, private-security operator, corporate enforcer, polished and hard-edged.
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the face of institutional menace: calm, articulate, and always one step away from a threat disguised as procedure. She’s not a cartoon villain; she’s a manager of damage, which makes her more dangerous in the school and conference-room scenes because she can sell coercion as empathy. The role has a great mix of authority, intelligence, and moral vacancy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Rebecca Ferguson in Dune or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers — a controlled, formidable operator whose power lives in precision rather than volume. It gives an actor a chance to play intelligence as intimidation.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: Male, elderly/90s in base form, shapeshifter, mentally fragmented, formerly a dementia patient.
lead_characters.hook: David is the script’s most tragic supporting figure: a broken old man whose identity has been splintered by the same experiment that made Madison. He’s tender, unstable, manipulative, and genuinely attached to Madison in a way that reads as both survival bond and emotional dependency. The role becomes haunting because he can be several people at once, but the emotional throughline is always loneliness and need.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Dano in The Fabelmans or John Lithgow in The Crown — a role built on vulnerability, instability, and sudden moral danger. It’s a rare chance to play age, fragility, and menace in one body.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, ex-military security operative, working-class, conflicted.
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the soldier inside the machine who still looks like he might have a conscience. He starts as part of the threat, but the script gives him enough human detail — the sick kid, the reluctance, the eventual turn — to make him more than a faceless enforcer. He’s useful because he keeps the security apparatus from feeling monolithic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Plemons in Breaking Bad or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire — a grounded, morally compromised operator who can flip from threat to ally. It’s a strong character-actor role with a late redemption lane.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, company nurse/handler, observant, professional, quietly sympathetic.
lead_characters.hook: Wilma is the softest face in the operation, which is exactly why she matters. She’s the one who can enter the school and the lab with a human tone, making the company’s coercion feel bureaucratic rather than monstrous until the script reveals how fully she’s inside the system. Her death lands because she’s been given enough humanity to matter.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Carrie Coon in The White Lotus or Jena Malone in The Neon Demon — a role that looks like support but carries real emotional shading. It gives an actor a chance to play competence, complicity, and vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, security lead, physically imposing, controlled, tactical.
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument of the operation: the guy with the earpiece, the gun, and the patience to keep the machine moving. He’s less psychologically rich than Priscilla or Wolcott, but he’s effective as the face of immediate physical danger and the one who keeps the chase engine moving. The role is all about controlled menace and tactical presence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Shea Whigham in any hard-edged crime role — a physically credible enforcer with enough personality to feel specific. It’s a clean, playable antagonist-supporting part.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 60s, scientist-executive, cold, clinical, intellectually arrogant.
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the script’s true ideological villain: the man who can talk about curing cancer and reversing aging while overseeing torture and body theft. He’s chilling because he believes in his own mission, which makes every line feel like a rationalization rather than a confession. The role is a great blend of corporate scientist and moral void.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Your Honor or Michael Keaton in Spotlight’s institutional authority lane — a role where intelligence becomes self-justifying cruelty. It gives an actor a chance to play polished evil without moustache-twirling.

supporting roles need distinct physicality and authority

technical.vfx_details: Body-shift transformations, skin bubbling, identity morphs, and a few practical-enhanced mutation moments; mostly character-facing rather than large-scale spectacle.
technical.sfx_needs: Foam spray effects, burns, fire ignition, cattle prods, gunfire, collapses, and practical transformation makeup/prosthetics.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original, specialty theatrical, or genre distributor with broad streaming afterlife

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep it contained, but the script still asks for a school, mall, forest, warehouse, secret lab, and multiple transformation-heavy sequences with fire and stunt work.

casting.note: The lead has to carry teen vulnerability, body-horror panic, and a late emotional reveal, while also playing multiple forms and identities; June, Priscilla, and David all need strong, specific actors to make the ensemble click.

development.note: The identity reveal and body-copy rules are the script’s engine, so the buyer has to buy the logic of memory transfer, form changes, and the Ava/Madison switch early.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Body-swap identity chaos and teen-comedy energy collide with real stakes, but this script pushes the concept into more emotional and conspiratorial territory.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre-forward viewers who like smart, emotional sci-fi thrillers with teen energy, identity stakes, and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 18-44, slightly female-leaning, with strong crossover to horror/sci-fi fans and streaming genre audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, a contained small-town footprint, and moderate transformation/VFX work keep this in indie-feature territory, though the climax adds fire, stunts, and effects pressure.

types_of_buyers: producer looking for a female-led high-concept feature
director seeking a contained but distinctive breakout vehicle
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where concept clarity matters as much as emotional payoff: a smart, propulsive genre feature with enough body-horror and identity drama to feel premium without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a complete emotional and plot resolution; the shapeshifter world is interesting, but the script does not build a clean sequel or spinoff vector beyond this story.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one breath: teen girl, secret experiment, shapeshifting, cover-up, survival. That makes it easy to pitch, easy to market, and easy for a director or actor to see the movie on the page.
strengths.evidence: The opening woods chase, the roadside shapeshift, and the later reveal that the girl is not who she thinks she is.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Identity is the engine, not just the gimmick.
strengths.what_it_means: The body-changing premise is tied to self-worth, class shame, and the fear of being unlovable, which gives the concept emotional durability. That’s what makes the script more than a creature feature and gives it awards-adjacent acting appeal.
strengths.evidence: Ava’s mirror scenes, the necklace as identity anchor, and the final note about not being made out of love.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother-daughter bond pays off hard.
strengths.what_it_means: June is not just support; she becomes the emotional and tactical co-anchor of the climax, which broadens the movie’s appeal beyond teen genre audiences. That gives the project a stronger commercial center and a better actor conversation for the mother role.
strengths.evidence: June revealing she can shapeshift too, the mall escape, and the final found-family coda.

strengths.what_it_means: Priscilla, David, Wilma, Mills, and Wolcott each bring a different pressure profile, so the movie can generate tension from multiple relationships rather than one chase line alone. That helps both casting and trailer construction.
strengths.evidence: The school confrontation, the conference-room reveal, and the warehouse/lab power shifts.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The climax is built for genre payoff.
strengths.what_it_means: The final act gives you body horror, fire, moral choice, and a clean emotional resolution, which is exactly what genre buyers want when they’re deciding whether a script can deliver. It’s the kind of ending that can make the whole package feel bigger than its budget.
strengths.evidence: The lab inferno, David’s sacrifice, Madison’s restoration, and the final road-trip escape.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable elevated sci-fi thriller with a real actor’s role at the center and a contained production footprint that keeps it inside indie-feature economics. The script’s best commercial asset is that it pairs a high-concept body-shift hook with a deeply emotional identity story, which gives buyers both a marketable genre engine and a performance-forward lead vehicle.

items.area: The identity reveal is a late buy-in.
items.detail: The script spends a long stretch operating as a straightforward shapeshifter chase before it reveals that Ava is actually Madison and that the real Ava exists separately. That twist is strong, but it means the audience has to trust the movie’s logic for a long time before the emotional architecture fully clicks.

The script has a lot of mechanics to track: touch-copying, memory bleed, foam suppression, form retention, age limits, and identity overwrite. That complexity is part of the appeal, but it also narrows the buyer pool to execs who are comfortable with a concept that needs careful explanation.

items.area: The climax leans hard on VFX and effects.
items.detail: The lab fire, foam ignition, skin mutation, bodybag reveals, and multiple transformation states all stack in the final stretch. It’s still an indie-scale feature, but the last act is where the budget and practical-effects plan will get tested the most.

Ava/Madison has to play teen insecurity, physical terror, comic timing, moral outrage, and then a full identity collapse without losing audience sympathy. That is a real lift, and the movie’s value rises or falls on whether the lead can make the emotional switchbacks feel inevitable.

items.area: The corporate conspiracy is broad by design.
items.detail: Eric, Priscilla, Wolcott, Jamieson, Mills, Wilma, the school, the mall, the lab, and the town all feed the same machine, but the operation is intentionally sprawling. That gives the movie scale, though it also means the script is asking the audience to accept a fairly large conspiracy apparatus inside a relatively intimate feature.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is that it asks the audience to track a fairly intricate identity system before the central Ava/Madison truth fully lands. The other pressure points are practical rather than fatal: a transformation-heavy climax and a lead role that needs a very specific kind of actor to make the whole thing sing.
